title: The shares
hook: the inheritance verses set shares for daughters, sons, parents, spouses (4:11–12)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the orphans' property, yatim, no swapping, no mixing, handed over with witnesses. Your line was theirs is theirs. Did you help an orphan cause? Day three hundred seventy-eight, the end of a week.

After Uhud, a widow came to the Prophet ﷺ with her two daughters. Their father, Sa'd ibn al-Rabi', had been killed in the battle. And their uncle had taken everything Sa'd owned. Commentators describe the old custom: the men who could fight inherited, and women and girls were left out. She asked the Prophet plainly: who will marry these girls with nothing? The reports say the inheritance verses came down soon after.
screen: `A WIDOW AND TWO DAUGHTERS.` → `THE UNCLE TOOK EVERYTHING.` → `WHO WILL CARE FOR THESE GIRLS?`

segments.voice: The word is mirath, inheritance, from a root meaning to inherit, to be left something. Verses 11 and 12 of an-Nisa set fixed shares, by name. Daughters inherit. Mothers inherit. Wives and husbands inherit from each other. Parents each receive a sixth when there are children. A husband receives half of his wife's estate if she has no children, a quarter if she does; a wife receives a quarter, or an eighth. Sisters and brothers have shares in certain cases. And before anything is divided, the verses repeat, any bequest is honored and debts are paid. In the story, the Prophet sent for the uncle and told him to give the daughters two-thirds, the mother an eighth, and keep the rest. A rule people often ask about is that a son receives twice the share of a daughter. Classical scholars explain it by duties: in Islamic law, a man must pay the bride's dower and support his wife and family, while a woman's wealth is her own, owed to no one. Some scholars also point out cases where a woman's share equals or exceeds a man's. Muslims today discuss how these rules apply in modern economies, and families and countries handle them in different ways. Another hadith, in Bukhari, adds a limit: a person may leave up to a third by will, and the Prophet said even a third is a lot. Better to leave your heirs well off than dependent. So the shares turned a family's money from whoever was strongest to a list where everyone has a place. Look back over this week: the message outliving the messenger, consultation, death tasted, the night sky, one soul, the orphans, and now the shares. A surah, and a week, about what we owe each other.
screen: `MIRATH: WHAT IS LEFT TO YOU` · `DAUGHTERS, MOTHERS, WIVES BY NAME` · `DEBTS FIRST, THEN THE SHARES` · `UP TO A THIRD BY WILL` · then, large: `EVERYONE HAS A SHARE.`

segments.voice: This one is practical, and it's an act of care. When the bell starts, think about what you'd leave behind if your time came. Not with fear. Just inventory. What do you own? What do you owe? Who depends on you? Is anything written down? Notice which answers you don't know. After the bell, write down one thing: where your important papers are, or who should get one thing you care about. The bell holds the time.
Mirath. Inheritance: the shares set out in 4:11 and 12 for daughters, sons, parents and spouses, after debts are paid. Today's word.
Your line: everyone has a share. Today, write down where your things should go, or start that conversation with your family. Day three hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Muslims divide estates according to the shares in 4:11–12 and 4:176, after debts and any bequest of up to a third; the detailed calculation is a field of Islamic law called 'ilm al-fara'id, and many Muslims write an Islamic will.

original.note: Arabic: inheritance, from the root w-r-th, to inherit.

trapdoor: what you thought: the son gets double, end of story.
what it means: fixed shares for daughters, mothers, wives and others, after debts, with up to a third by will.
what a scholar hears: the occasion of Sa'd ibn al-Rabi''s daughters; the classical link between shares and men's duty of maintenance; and cases where women's shares equal or exceed men's.
